screens.title: Control Flow: Conditional Statements
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow is how a program decides what to run next. In Python, conditional statements let your program choose between different actions based on a condition. You will learn how to write if, elif, and else branches, why indentation defines code blocks in Python, how to combine checks with logical operators, and what values Python treats as true or false. These tools let your application react to user input, validate data, and route logic without repeating code. For example, a login check uses a conditional to accept or reject credentials; a game story uses nested decisions to branch the narrative; and a data-processing script uses truthiness to skip empty inputs. We'll practice safe patterns, spot common mistakes such as using the assignment operator where a comparison is needed, and practice concise checks like the ternary expression. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to express conditional logic clearly, avoid indentation errors, and choose readable strategies for multiple branches. Think about a real decision you make daily—conditional statements let your code make decisions the same way.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice so you can write conditional logic that is correct and readable. First, you will implement conditional logic using if, elif, and else to route execution. That means you will write branches that check conditions and run the intended code only when those conditions hold. Second, you will understand the critical role of indentation in Python. Indentation defines blocks of code; if you mis-indent, Python either raises an error or changes program behavior. You will practice consistent four-space indentation and see how nested blocks depend on alignment. Third, you will combine multiple conditions using and, or, and not. These operators let you express compound rules like checking age and consent together. Finally, you will recognize and use Python's truthiness and falsiness concepts so you can check containers, numbers, and optional values concisely. Each skill is paired with a small verified milestone to confirm mastery: a short script or a set of unit-test checks. These competencies map directly to writing safe input checks, branching game logic, and concise data validation in real programs.

screens.title: What is a conditional statement?
screens.narratorSegment: A conditional statement tells a program to run a block of code only when a test is true. The most basic conditional is the if statement: it evaluates a condition, and if that condition holds, the indented block beneath it executes. An elif clause provides an additional test after the initial if; Python evaluates these in order and runs only the first block whose condition is true. The else clause runs when every preceding condition is false. Think of this as a single-choice decision: the first matching branch wins. For example, when grading a numeric score you might check if the score is at least ninety, else if it is at least eighty, else if it is at least seventy, otherwise fail. This ordering matters: a higher threshold must be tested before a lower one so the intended grade is chosen. A common misconception is to assume all matching blocks run; in a chained if-elif-else only one branch executes. Another confusion arises when using separate if statements instead of elif; separate ifs will each be evaluated independently and can all run, changing logic unintentionally. Takeaway: structure checks in the correct order so only the intended block executes. How will you order checks for inclusive ranges in your next script?

keyIdea.title: Single-choice branching
keyIdea.text: In an if-elif-else chain, the first true condition executes and the rest are skipped. Order your checks from most specific to most general.

content.html:
Core Concept
If, Elif, Else
A chain of tests where the first true branch runs once. Maintain ordering from specific to general.
Explanation
  • if evaluates a condition and runs its indented block only when true.
  • elif provides an additional test only reached if previous conditions were false.
  • else runs when no prior tests succeeded, acting as a default path.
Concrete example
Grade selection based on numeric score using descending thresholds.
Key Takeaway

Order matters. Use elif when you want mutually exclusive branches and avoid separate ifs for the same decision.

Code example
score = 85
if score >= 90:
  print("Grade: A")
elif score >= 80:
  print("Grade: B")
elif score >= 70:
  print("Grade: C")
else:
  print("Grade: F")
Misconception
Using separate if statements here would allow multiple prints; use elif to enforce exclusivity.

screens.title: Indentation: the block delimiter
screens.narratorSegment: In Python, indentation is not just style — it defines which statements belong together. A colon after an if or else introduces a block that must be indented consistently. Typical style uses four spaces per indent level. If indentation is inconsistent, Python raises an IndentationError or, worse, code runs with different logical grouping than you intend. For example, placing a print statement with the wrong indentation can move it outside a conditional or tie it to a different if. A common beginner mistake is mixing tabs and spaces, which can look correct but fail at runtime. Configure your editor to insert spaces and reveal whitespace so you can see levels. When you nest conditionals, keep each level aligned; deeply nested logic becomes hard to read and is a sign to refactor into helper functions. Practice: deliberately write a short conditional, then re-indent the inner block to see how behavior changes. Misunderstanding indentation often causes subtle bugs, so learning to read blocks visually is as important as writing them. How will you check indentation in your editor next time? Indentation: the block delimiter means consistent spaces define code blocks. use four spaces, avoid mixing tabs, and refactor deep nesting into functions.. In practical terms, why whitespace defines code structure in python and how to avoid errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Indentation rule
keyIdea.text: Consistent spaces define code blocks. Use four spaces, avoid mixing tabs, and refactor deep nesting into functions.

content.html:
Definition
Indentation matters
Blocks are formed by consistent indentation. Misaligned lines change which code runs together and often cause errors.
Common mistakes
  • Mixing tabs and spaces; use spaces only.
  • Incorrect indentation level that moves statements out of blocks.
  • Excessive nesting that reduces readability.
Common mistake

An IndentationError or altered logic often indicates inconsistent spacing or a misplaced line.

Example and check
if user_is_admin:
    print("Welcome, admin")
    print("You have full access")
print("This always runs")
If the final print is indented, it would run only for admins. Keep block levels visually consistent. Configure your editor to show invisible characters and set tabs to insert spaces.

screens.title: Evaluation order in if-elif-else chains
screens.narratorSegment: Python evaluates an if-elif-else chain from top to bottom and stops after the first true branch. This evaluation strategy means the order of conditions determines which block runs when multiple conditions could be true. For example, if you test for a general condition first, a more specific later condition will never be reached. Use descending thresholds or specificity-first ordering to avoid hidden bugs. A useful mental model is short-circuit evaluation for the chain: once a branch is selected, subsequent checks are skipped entirely. Many learners mistakenly think all boolean expressions are evaluated before any branch runs; they are not. This also has a performance implication: place cheaper checks earlier if they often fail, or place the most likely true checks early to avoid unnecessary work. When you combine conditions with logical operators inside a test, Python short-circuits within that expression as well — for and and or, evaluation may stop early. Takeaway: order conditions intentionally for correctness and efficiency. Which condition in your code should be tested first to reflect real-world priorities? Evaluation order in if-elif-else chains means python picks the first true branch and skips the rest. order conditions from most specific or likely to match to the least.. In practical terms, how python checks conditions and short-circuits the chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Top-to-bottom selection
keyIdea.text: Python picks the first true branch and skips the rest. Order conditions from most specific or likely to match to the least.

content.html:
Process Flow
Top-to-bottom evaluation
Conditions are checked in order. The first true condition executes and the rest are skipped, which affects both correctness and performance.
Step 1
Evaluate the if condition. If true, run block and stop.
Step 2
If the if was false, evaluate each elif in order until one is true.
Step 3
If none matched and an else exists, run else as a default.
Example — importance of order
score = 85
# Wrong: general check first hides specific result
if score >= 70:
  print("Passed")
elif score >= 80:
  print("Good")

# Correct: specific to general
if score >= 90:
  print("A")
elif score >= 80:
  print("B")
Misconception: placing a broad condition early can prevent more precise logic from running. Order is both a correctness and readability tool.

screens.title: Logical operators: and, or, not
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine simple tests into expressive conditions. Use and to require that both sub-conditions are true, or to allow either sub-condition, and not to invert a condition. For example, to allow access only when a user is old enough and has parental consent, combine the checks with and. A common pitfall is misunderstanding precedence: and has higher precedence than or, so parenthesis can clarify intent and avoid subtle bugs. Another pitfall is overusing nested ifs where combining conditions would be clearer. Additionally, short-circuit behavior matters: with and, if the first part is false Python won't evaluate the second part; with or, if the first part is true the second part is skipped. This affects side effects if the second part calls a function. When you need to check membership and negate it, use not before the condition rather than reversing complex logic inside. Concrete example: check weather and rain flag to decide whether to picnic. Misconception: thinking or returns a boolean only—in Python it returns one of the operands; rely on truthiness rather than expecting a strict True or False in some expressions. Close by practicing combining checks and wrapping complex groups with parentheses.

keyIdea.title: Combine and invert
keyIdea.text: and requires both, or requires one, and not inverts. Use parentheses to make precedence explicit and avoid unexpected short-circuit effects.

content.html:
Comparison
and, or, not
Use these operators to express compound conditions without deep nesting.
and
True only if both parts are true. Short-circuits on first false.
or
True if either part is true. Short-circuits on first true.
not
Inverts truth value; use to negate a condition cleanly.
Tip
Use parentheses to group complex expressions and avoid precedence surprises.
Concrete example
temperature = 25
is_raining = True

if temperature > 20 and not is_raining:
  print("Perfect day for a picnic")
elif temperature > 20 and is_raining:
  print("Warm but raining; indoor options")
else:
  print("Chilly or cloudy; stay warm")
Misconception: expect and/or to always return True or False. They return one of the operands; use them with truthiness in mind.

screens.title: Truthiness and falsiness
screens.narratorSegment: Truthiness is the rule Python uses to treat non-boolean values as True or False in conditions. Falsy values include False, None, zero numeric values, and empty containers like empty strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. Everything else is truthy. This behavior lets you write concise checks: instead of checking length greater than zero, you can write if my_list to run code only when the list is non-empty. A common confusion is thinking that a list containing zero is falsy; it is truthy because it is not empty. Another point is that numeric zero is falsy, which matters when distinguishing between an empty container and a zero value. When you rely on truthiness, ensure the meaning is clear to readers; for critical logic prefer explicit comparisons if ambiguity could cause bugs. For example, when an empty string and zero mean different things in your domain, test explicitly. Practice by converting a few explicit comparisons into truthiness checks and run tests to confirm behavior. Takeaway: use truthiness to write cleaner conditions, but prefer explicit checks when values have domain-specific meanings. Truthiness and falsiness means empty containers, zero, none, and false are falsy. use truthiness for concise checks, but prefer explicit tests when values carry different semantic meanings.. In practical terms, which values evaluate to false and how to leverage that behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Falsy list
keyIdea.text: Empty containers, zero, None, and False are falsy. Use truthiness for concise checks, but prefer explicit tests when values carry different semantic meanings.

content.html:
Definition
Truthiness and Falsiness
Python treats certain non-boolean values as false in boolean contexts. Knowing which ones saves comparisons.
Common falsy values
  • False, None
  • 0, 0.0
  • "" (empty string)
  • [] , (), {}, set() (empty containers)
Pro tip

Use direct truthiness checks for brevity, but test explicitly when zero and empty mean different things.

Examples
if my_list:
  print("List has items")

if not user_input:
  print("No input provided")

# Numeric zero is falsy
if score:
  print("Non-zero score")
else:
  print("Score is zero or missing")
Misconception: a list containing zero is truthy. It's non-empty, so the direct check will be true.

screens.title: The pass statement and placeholders
screens.narratorSegment: The pass statement performs no operation; it exists so a block can be syntactically present when you plan to implement logic later. Use pass in an if or else branch as a placeholder while you build other parts of the program. This keeps the interpreter from raising an error for an empty block. A typical workflow is to sketch out conditional branches with pass in each block, then fill them progressively. However, do not leave pass statements in production code where the branch should perform meaningful work — they can hide missing logic and lead to silent failures. Another common pattern is to raise a NotImplementedError in branches that must not remain unimplemented. Use pass when the empty behavior is intentional for now, and add a clear TODO comment. Example: writing scaffolding for a game where several game states are planned; using pass lets you run the program while implementing one state at a time. Takeaway: pass keeps the code runnable during incremental development but should be replaced with real logic before release. The pass statement and placeholders means pass provides a no-op block so code remains syntactically correct during incremental development. replace with real logic before shipping.. In practical terms, using pass to keep syntactically valid but unfinished branches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
pass — a no-op placeholder
Use pass to keep a block present when logic is unfinished. It's a development aid, not a final behavior.
When to use
  • Sketching program flow before implementation.
  • Keeping conditionals syntactically valid while building other parts.
Example
if feature_enabled:
  # TODO: implement advanced path
  pass
else:
  print("Default behavior")
Pro tip: add a TODO comment or raise an explicit exception if the branch must not remain unimplemented.

screens.title: Conditional expression (ternary)
screens.narratorSegment: Python provides a concise conditional expression to select a value based on a condition. It uses the form value_if_true if condition else value_if_false and is useful for short assignments that would otherwise require a multi-line if-else. For example, you can assign a status string based on age in a single line. This makes simple choices cleaner and keeps variable assignment local and readable. Avoid using the conditional expression for complex side-effecting logic or for chains of conditions; then a normal if-elif-else is clearer. screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: Many conditional bugs come from a few predictable mistakes. First, confusing assignment and comparison is frequent in other languages; in Python use the assignment operator to store values and the equality comparison operator to compare values. While Python's syntax discourages the exact assignment-in-condition bug found elsewhere, developers still misread code and mix up intended semantics. Second, indentation errors either raise exceptions or subtly change program flow; an unexpected IndentationError is a clear sign to check spacing. Third, overly nested if-elif-else structures become hard to reason about and are more error-prone; refactor to functions or use combined conditions to flatten logic. Fourth, assuming truthiness on a variable without understanding its possible values can hide edge cases—explicit checks are safer when input semantics matter. Debugging habits: run small inputs, add print diagnostics that state which branch executed, and write unit tests for each branch. Use linters and editor settings to reveal whitespace and to warn about suspicious comparisons. Practicing these checks and tests prevents the majority of conditional-related bugs. fullNarratorScript:
Control flow is how a program decides what to run next. In Python, conditional statements let your program choose between different actions based on a condition. You will learn how to write if, elif, and else branches, why indentation defines code blocks in Python, how to combine checks with logical operators, and what values Python treats as true or false. These tools let your application react to user input, validate data, and route logic without repeating code. For example, a login check uses a conditional to accept or reject credentials; a game story uses nested decisions to branch the narrative; and a data-processing script uses truthiness to skip empty inputs. We'll practice safe patterns, spot common mistakes such as using the assignment operator where a comparison is needed, and practice concise checks like the ternary expression. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to express conditional logic clearly, avoid indentation errors, and choose readable strategies for multiple branches. Think about a real decision you make daily—conditional statements let your code make decisions the same way.

These objectives focus your practice so you can write conditional logic that is correct and readable. First, you will implement conditional logic using if, elif, and else to route execution. That means you will write branches that check conditions and run the intended code only when those conditions hold. Second, you will understand the critical role of indentation in Python. Indentation defines blocks of code; if you mis-indent, Python either raises an error or changes program behavior. You will practice consistent four-space indentation and see how nested blocks depend on alignment. Third, you will combine multiple conditions using and, or, and not. These operators let you express compound rules like checking age and consent together. Finally, you will recognize and use Python's truthiness and falsiness concepts so you can check containers, numbers, and optional values concisely. Each skill is paired with a small verified milestone to confirm mastery: a short script or a set of unit-test checks. These competencies map directly to writing safe input checks, branching game logic, and concise data validation in real programs.

This follow-up objectives slide frames the same four outcomes as practice tasks and verification steps. First, implement conditional logic: you will create short scripts that branch based on input and pass tests that assert correct outputs for sample inputs. Second, demonstrate correct indentation by submitting code where block boundaries are clear and no indentation errors occur. Third, combine conditions: build examples that use and and or to require multiple checks, and use not to invert a condition when that simplifies logic. Fourth, apply truthiness and falsiness: write checks that rely on empty containers evaluating to false rather than manually comparing lengths. Each milestone trains habits that prevent common bugs: predictable ordering of branches, consistent four-space indentation, avoiding deep nesting when a logical operator would suffice, and writing idiomatic concise checks. These habits make code easier to read and debug, and prepare you to refactor nested branches into clearer, maintainable code.

A conditional statement tells a program to run a block of code only when a test is true. The most basic conditional is the if statement: it evaluates a condition, and if that condition holds, the indented block beneath it executes. An elif clause provides an additional test after the initial if; Python evaluates these in order and runs only the first block whose condition is true. The else clause runs when every preceding condition is false. Think of this as a single-choice decision: the first matching branch wins. For example, when grading a numeric score you might check if the score is at least ninety, else if it is at least eighty, else if it is at least seventy, otherwise fail. This ordering matters: a higher threshold must be tested before a lower one so the intended grade is chosen. A common misconception is to assume all matching blocks run; in a chained if-elif-else only one branch executes. Another confusion arises when using separate if statements instead of elif; separate ifs will each be evaluated independently and can all run, changing logic unintentionally. Takeaway: structure checks in the correct order so only the intended block executes. How will you order checks for inclusive ranges in your next script?

In Python, indentation is not just style — it defines which statements belong together. A colon after an if or else introduces a block that must be indented consistently. Typical style uses four spaces per indent level. If indentation is inconsistent, Python raises an IndentationError or, worse, code runs with different logical grouping than you intend. For example, placing a print statement with the wrong indentation can move it outside a conditional or tie it to a different if. A common beginner mistake is mixing tabs and spaces, which can look correct but fail at runtime. Configure your editor to insert spaces and reveal whitespace so you can see levels. When you nest conditionals, keep each level aligned; deeply nested logic becomes hard to read and is a sign to refactor into helper functions. Practice: deliberately write a short conditional, then re-indent the inner block to see how behavior changes. Misunderstanding indentation often causes subtle bugs, so learning to read blocks visually is as important as writing them. How will you check indentation in your editor next time? Indentation: the block delimiter means consistent spaces define code blocks. use four spaces, avoid mixing tabs, and refactor deep nesting into functions.. In practical terms, why whitespace defines code structure in python and how to avoid errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Python evaluates an if-elif-else chain from top to bottom and stops after the first true branch. This evaluation strategy means the order of conditions determines which block runs when multiple conditions could be true. For example, if you test for a general condition first, a more specific later condition will never be reached. Use descending thresholds or specificity-first ordering to avoid hidden bugs. A useful mental model is short-circuit evaluation for the chain: once a branch is selected, subsequent checks are skipped entirely. Many learners mistakenly think all boolean expressions are evaluated before any branch runs; they are not. This also has a performance implication: place cheaper checks earlier if they often fail, or place the most likely true checks early to avoid unnecessary work. When you combine conditions with logical operators inside a test, Python short-circuits within that expression as well — for and and or, evaluation may stop early. Takeaway: order conditions intentionally for correctness and efficiency. Which condition in your code should be tested first to reflect real-world priorities? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logical operators let you combine simple tests into expressive conditions. Use and to require that both sub-conditions are true, or to allow either sub-condition, and not to invert a condition. For example, to allow access only when a user is old enough and has parental consent, combine the checks with and. A common pitfall is misunderstanding precedence: and has higher precedence than or, so parenthesis can clarify intent and avoid subtle bugs. Another pitfall is overusing nested ifs where combining conditions would be clearer. Additionally, short-circuit behavior matters: with and, if the first part is false Python won't evaluate the second part; with or, if the first part is true the second part is skipped. This affects side effects if the second part calls a function. When you need to check membership and negate it, use not before the condition rather than reversing complex logic inside. Concrete example: check weather and rain flag to decide whether to picnic. Misconception: thinking or returns a boolean only—in Python it returns one of the operands; rely on truthiness rather than expecting a strict True or False in some expressions. Close by practicing combining checks and wrapping complex groups with parentheses.

Truthiness is the rule Python uses to treat non-boolean values as True or False in conditions. Falsy values include False, None, zero numeric values, and empty containers like empty strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. Everything else is truthy. This behavior lets you write concise checks: instead of checking length greater than zero, you can write if my_list to run code only when the list is non-empty. A common confusion is thinking that a list containing zero is falsy; it is truthy because it is not empty. Another point is that numeric zero is falsy, which matters when distinguishing between an empty container and a zero value. When you rely on truthiness, ensure the meaning is clear to readers; for critical logic prefer explicit comparisons if ambiguity could cause bugs. For example, when an empty string and zero mean different things in your domain, test explicitly. Practice by converting a few explicit comparisons into truthiness checks and run tests to confirm behavior. The pass statement performs no operation; it exists so a block can be syntactically present when you plan to implement logic later. Use pass in an if or else branch as a placeholder while you build other parts of the program. This keeps the interpreter from raising an error for an empty block. A typical workflow is to sketch out conditional branches with pass in each block, then fill them progressively.
